text:
Keep the Joined-Up Hand

Every few years someone proposes that primary schools should stop teaching joined-up handwriting. The argument sounds reasonable. Children type on tablets before they can tie their shoes, adults write by hand only for shopping lists and birthday cards, and classroom hours are scarce. Why spend months drilling loops and exit strokes when a keyboard will do the job faster and more legibly? I think the argument is wrong. Primary schools should keep teaching cursive, or at least a fluent joined script, as a core skill. The case rests on three things: what the hand does for the developing mind, what fluent writing does for a child's ability to think on paper, and what is lost when a society decides a skill is too old-fashioned to hand on.

Begin with the brain. Writing by hand is not typing slowed down. When a child forms a letter, the hand must plan a shape, control pressure, sequence several strokes and judge the result by eye. A key press, by contrast, is the same small motion for every letter. Researchers who have scanned the brains of children and adults while they wrote or typed have repeatedly found more widespread activity in the handwriting condition, especially in regions tied to memory and learning. A well known set of studies compared children who learned letters by writing them with those who learned by typing or tracing. The writers recognised letters more reliably and showed stronger activation in reading related areas afterward. The finding is not that handwriting makes children cleverer in general. It is that the physical act of making a letter helps fix that letter in memory, which is exactly what a six year old needs.

Joined writing adds something further. Printing is a series of separate stops and starts, each letter a fresh decision. A joined script turns a word into one continuous movement. The child learns that a word is a unit, not a pile of parts, and that spelling has a rhythm. Teachers of children with spelling difficulties often report that cursive helps, because the hand learns common letter strings as patterns and can carry them without conscious effort. Some specialists in dyslexia recommend joined writing for this reason, and for a second one too. In print, children confuse letters that are mirror images of each other, such as b and d. In a joined script those letters begin and end differently, so the confusion shrinks. A skill that quietly helps the pupils who struggle most is not a luxury.

The second argument concerns speed and thought. The critics of handwriting say the keyboard is faster, and for an adult touch typist it is. But a child of eight is nowhere near that point, and keyboard skill takes years to build. Meanwhile a child who has to print every letter separately writes slowly, tires quickly and loses the thread of the sentence before the pen catches up. Fluent joined writing is the quickest way to get thoughts onto a page without any device. Studies of children's composition have found a strong link between handwriting fluency and the quality and length of their written work. When the mechanics demand attention, less attention is left for ideas, vocabulary and structure. Once the mechanics are automatic, the mind is free. The goal of teaching cursive is not pretty pages. It is to make the act of writing cheap enough that a child will actually do it.

There is also the matter of examinations. Many national tests, and almost all public examinations in the later years of school, are still written by hand and will remain so for the foreseeable future, because paper is cheap, secure and does not run out of battery. A pupil who cannot write quickly and legibly for two hours is at a disadvantage in every subject, not just in English. Teachers who mark scripts see the difference plainly. A neat, steady joined hand lets an examiner follow an argument. A slow, cramped or illegible one costs marks that have nothing to do with knowledge. A school that drops handwriting instruction in primary years is making a bet that this situation will change by the time its pupils sit their exams. That is a risky bet to place on behalf of children who cannot place it themselves.

Now consider the best objection: time. The school day is finite, and every minute for handwriting is a minute not spent on reading, mathematics or coding. This is true, but the numbers are smaller than critics suggest. Handwriting instruction in good schools takes short daily sessions, often ten or fifteen minutes, spread over a few years. Compared with the hours spent on screens, the cost is modest. And the time is not wasted even by the critics' own standard, since the same sessions train fine motor control, attention and patience, qualities that screens rarely demand. If the real concern is crowded timetables, the answer is to protect the short, regular practice that works, not to abandon the subject altogether.

A second objection is that print is clearer and that most adults in fact write a hybrid anyway. That is partly right, and it points to a sensible way of teaching rather than a reason to stop. No one needs to demand the elaborate looped capitals of a nineteenth century copybook. Modern schools can teach a simple, economical joined script, with plain letter shapes and short exit strokes, and let each pupil develop a personal style from it. That is how most adults end up writing anyway. The hybrid is the product of having learned a joined system first and then loosening it. Take away the foundation and there is nothing to loosen. Adults who never learned to join letters often describe their writing as childish and slow, and they do not usually feel they chose that.

A third objection is that handwriting is unfair to children with motor difficulties. This deserves a serious answer, because some pupils find writing painful. But the right response is support, not removal for everyone. Children with significant motor problems should have access to keyboards and other tools, and schools should provide them without stigma. That accommodation depends on a baseline that everyone else is taught. We do not abolish swimming lessons because some children cannot swim easily, and we do not stop teaching reading because some find it hard. We adapt for the child and keep the curriculum.

Beyond the practical arguments there is a cultural one, and I do not think it should be waved away as sentiment. Joined handwriting is how generations have recorded their lives. Letters, diaries, recipes, wartime postcards and the margins of old books are all written in cursive. A child who cannot read it cannot read a grandparent's letter or a historical document in an archive without a translator. It is a little odd to speak of the importance of heritage and primary sources while leaving a generation unable to read them. Teaching children to read and write a joined hand is cheap insurance against becoming strangers to our own written past.

There is also something to be said for the dignity of the personal mark. A signature, a note left on a kitchen table, a card written to a friend in hospital: these carry a trace of the person that typed text does not. Children sense this. Ask a class who would prefer to receive a handwritten note and a typed message, and the notes win. A school that teaches handwriting teaches children a way of giving something of themselves, which no font can imitate.

None of this means schools should ignore keyboards. Typing is a vital skill and should be taught explicitly, starting in the later primary years, with proper technique, not left to chance. The sensible position is both, in the right order. Children first learn to write by hand, which builds letter knowledge, fluency and fine control, and then add keyboarding once the foundations are secure. Countries that dropped handwriting hastily have in some cases changed course. Several American states that had removed cursive from their curricula have restored it in recent years, and in Scandinavia, where digital teaching was pursued with enthusiasm, policymakers have pushed to bring back pens, paper and printed books after concerns about falling reading and writing standards. When systems that went furthest toward screens start moving back, it is wise to listen.

So the answer is yes. Primary schools should keep teaching joined-up handwriting, in a modern, simple form, with short daily practice and proper support for children who struggle. It strengthens memory for letters, speeds the flow of composition, helps pupils who find spelling and reading hard, prepares children for handwritten examinations, and keeps open the door to the written record of the past. The cost is small and the benefits are broad. The keyboard is a wonderful tool, but a tool is best used by someone who has first learned what the hand can do on its own.
